# Jeremiah 49: Research notes for a verse-by-verse commentary

**How to read these notes:** I ran out of search and fetch requests before I could read sources for every verse. Verses 33 and 36–37 have only a little material. I found nothing on the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Pentecostal-denominational, NET Bible or Bible Odyssey sites. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Most older commentators (Gill, Calvin, Clarke, Henry, Ellicott, Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch) were reached through the BibleHub and StudyLight collections. Points taken from the two full pages I fetched (Gill's commentary and Enduring Word) carry their URLs but no citation tags.

---

## Ammon (vv. 1–6)

**v. 1**
- **Guzik:** Ammon had moved into land given to Gad, Reuben and Manasseh. It lived there in the name of its god Milcom, as if Israel's inheritance no longer counted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Kidner (quoted by Guzik):** Milcom is Molech, worshipped with child sacrifice. Naming the god as the invader lifts the issue "above the political." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Gill:** "Israel" here means all Israel. Judah and Benjamin were the next of kin and so the rightful heirs after the ten tribes were exiled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html
- **Calvin:** God tolerated the theft for a while but would not let Ammon go unpunished. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-49.html
- **"Their king" or "Milcom"?**
  - Pulpit: the ancient Greek, Syriac and Latin translations read "Milcom". The difference lies only in the vowel marks. The actual vowel points give "malcam", which could also mean Ammon's earthly king. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-49.html
  - Keil & Delitzsch: Jeremiah, echoing Amos 1:15, uses מלכּם in a double sense. In v. 1 it means mainly the human king; the god only clearly comes in at v. 3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-1.htm

**v. 2**
- **Gill:** The war cry is the Chaldean army. Citing Josephus, he says Nebuchadnezzar conquered Ammon about five years after Jerusalem fell. The "daughters" are Rabbah's villages. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html
- **How "Israel will drive out their dispossessors" is fulfilled is where readings differ:**
  - Gill (Baptist): partly fulfilled after the return from exile and under the Maccabees. More fully fulfilled in the latter day, when the Jews shall be converted, and return to their own land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html
  - Calvin (Reformed): Israel never held that land, so the prophecy was not fully accomplished except under the kingdom of Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-49.html
  - Guzik: quotes Thompson that this did not happen in history, and suggests it may still be unfulfilled. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Matthew Henry:** we should recognise God's fairness when the losses of the injured are recompensed out of the unjust gains of the injurious. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_049.cfm

**v. 3**
- **Gill:** Heshbon was a Moabite city near Ammon's border. This Ai is an Ammonite town, not Joshua's Ai. "Their king" is better taken as the god Milcom, since priests are mentioned next. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html
- **Calvin:** The call to put on sackcloth is not a call to repent. Unbelievers copied the rituals of the faithful without discretion or judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-49.html
- **Guzik:** Babylon carrying off Milcom shows that the LORD is King of all the earth, not just a national god. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/

**v. 4**
- **Gill on the valleys:** Ammon took pride in its fertile valleys. Some Jewish commentators read "your valley flows" as flowing with the blood of the slain.
- **Gill on "faithless daughter":** Ammon descended from righteous Lot and worshipped idols, so the name fits. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html
- **Henry:** all idolaters may be called backsliders, because worship of the true God came before false gods. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_049.cfm
- **Guzik:** Ammon trusted its geography and its treasures. Both would fail. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/

**v. 5**
- **Gill:** The "terror" is the Chaldean army. Each person would flee straight ahead without looking back for family. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html

**v. 6**
- **Gill:**
  - The return was perhaps under Cyrus.
  - Ammon was a large people again in the Maccabean period.
  - Some apply the verse to Gentiles converting to the gospel.
  - Jewish interpreters apply it to Ammonite converts to Judaism.

  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html
- **G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik):** the ultimate purpose of the activity of wrath is that of restoration. Where no restoration is promised, that shows it is possible to resist even God's judgments. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/

## Edom (vv. 7–22)

**v. 7**
- **Thompson (quoted by Guzik):** Teman is a poetic name for Edom.
- **Guzik:** God judges a nation partly by giving it foolish leaders.
- **Morgan (quoted by Guzik):** this may be a dig at Eliphaz, Job's adviser, who came from Teman.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Gill:** Kimchi and Abarbanel apply "Edom" to Rome, and Cocceius applies it to the Jews. Gill prefers the literal Edomites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html
- **Constable:** Jeremiah draws heavily on Obadiah in this section. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-49.html

**v. 8**
- **Guzik on "dwell deep" (KJV):** Preachers, including F. B. Meyer, have used it as a call to "dwell deep" in God. That is valid as application but is not Jeremiah's meaning: it means digging in for shelter. It may be sarcasm or a real warning.
- **Guzik on "the calamity of Esau":** it recalls Esau losing everything when the birthright went to Jacob.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Calvin:** Edom was too proud to move when warned to flee. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-49.html

**v. 9**
- **Calvin:** Interpreters went wrong here by not comparing Obadiah: Obadiah is the true interpreter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-49.html
- **Gill:** Grape pickers and thieves always leave something. The Chaldeans would leave Edom nothing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html

**v. 10**
- **Gill:** "Brothers" means Ammon and Moab; "neighbours" means the Philistines. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html

**v. 11 (who is speaking, and is this hope?)**
- **Clarke:** The connexion of this with the context is not easy to be discerned, but widows and orphans are God's special care. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-49.html
- **Gill lists several readings:**
  - No one would be left to offer this kindness.
  - God is speaking ironically.
  - A remnant of Edom would be converted in gospel times.
  - The Targum applies the verse to Israel.

  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html
- **Guzik:** a glimmer of hope for Edom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Pulpit:** the promise implies a future for the race. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-49.html
- **Henry:** dying believers can leave their families in God's care. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_049.cfm

**v. 12**
- **Calvin:** Israel did deserve its suffering. The phrase is comparative and points to God's grace toward Israel. The cup is God's measured punishment. For believers, he says, present troubles purifies us now by temporal punishments so they escape final vengeance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-49.html
- **Gill:** "Those who do not deserve to drink" means either less guilty nations or the Jews. If judgment begins with God's own people, Edom cannot escape. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html

**v. 13**
- **Gill:** God swears by himself because he could swear by no greater. The Bozrah meant is Edom's, not Moab's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html
- **Feinberg (quoted by Guzik):** Bozrah was Edom's capital, between Petra and the Dead Sea. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/

**v. 14**
- **Clarke:** God revealed this to Jeremiah. The "envoy" means God has stirred up the hearts of these nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-49.html

**vv. 15–16**
- **Guzik:** Edom trusted its fierce soldiers and its high, defensible land.
- **Thompson (quoted by Guzik):** the rare word translated "terror" may be a mocking substitute for an Edomite god's name.
- **Feinberg (quoted by Guzik):** "the rock" is Sela, later called Petra.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/

**vv. 17–18**
- **Gill:** "No one will dwell there" means no Edomite; conquerors could and did live there. The picture alludes to the Dead Sea cities. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html

**v. 19**
- **Calvin:** the lion stands for the Chaldeans, like lions driven uphill when the Jordan floods. Edom is the helpless flock. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-19.html
- **"The chosen one":**
  - Ellicott: most commentators take it as Nebuchadnezzar. Ellicott himself reads it as scorn, asking who could be Edom's champion. The implied answer is that Edom has no such champion.
  - Matthew Poole: the lion is Edom itself.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-19.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** these are general truths, so the "chosen one" should not be tied to Nebuchadnezzar or Alexander. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-19.htm
- **BibleHub study notes:** see Babylon's king in the near term and Christ ultimately. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/49-19.htm

**v. 20**
- **Henry:** "the little ones of the flock" can mean even the weakest followers in Nebuchadnezzar's camp will drag Edom away. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_049.cfm

**v. 21**
- **Clarke:** Edom falls like a huge building, shaking the ground. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-49.html
- **Gill:** the cry is heard as far as the coast. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-49.html

**v. 22**
- **Guzik:** Edom thought itself as high as an eagle (v. 16), but God sends a greater eagle against it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/

## Damascus (vv. 23–27)

**v. 23**
- **Calvin:** "Damascus" stands for the whole kingdom of Syria, Israel's long-standing enemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-49.html
- **Feinberg (quoted by Guzik):** the "sea" must be figurative, since Syria had no coastline. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Jamieson, Fausset & Brown:** Assyria destroyed the kingdom, but the city revived, and this prophecy is about the city. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_049.cfm

**v. 24**
- **Henry:** a city that thought it could face any enemy now flees, as unable to fight its fate as a woman in labour. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_049.cfm

**v. 25 (a hard verse: what "not forsaken" means)**
- **Calvin:** "left" means spared: how could such a famous city not be spared? https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-25.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch (following Nägelsbach):** the point is that the people did not flee and so died in the city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-25.htm
- **Barnes:** "my joy" shows the prophet's own sympathy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-25.htm
- **Henry:** it was a city of praise to itself, not to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/jeremiah/49.htm
- **Guzik:** God honours the city and says it will not be emptied like others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Coffman:** the prophecy never calls Damascus a waste. He treats its survival to this day as evidence the prophecies come from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-25.html
- **Critical scholarship (Cambridge Bible):** the negative reverses the expected sense, so Duhm and Cornill alter the Hebrew text to read "Woe to her!" or "Woe to me!". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-25.htm

**vv. 26–27**
- **Coffman:** v. 27 is almost identical to Amos 1:4. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-25.html
- **Henry:** some think "Ben-hadad" was a common title for Syrian kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-25.html

## Kedar and Hazor (vv. 28–33)

**v. 28**
- **Henry:** Kedar descended from Ishmael. Hazor's people were perhaps Canaanites from the old kingdom of Hazor who settled in Arabia. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_049.cfm
- **Guzik:** this is probably not the Canaanite city Joshua conquered, though he links it with Judges 4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/

**v. 29**
- **Clarke:** the tents and flocks show these were nomadic Arabs whose wealth was livestock, especially camels. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-49.html

**vv. 30–31**
- **Henry:**
  - They were "wealthy" because they were content with enough.
  - Doing no wrong to others does not protect against men like Nebuchadnezzar.
  - Though he acted unjustly, God was righteous in directing it.

  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_049.cfm

**v. 32**
- **Guzik:** trimming the hair at the temples was forbidden in Leviticus 19:27. It may refer to Arab tribes who did this to honour a god, as Herodotus reports. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/

**v. 33**
- **Guzik:** Hazor, though wealthy, would become a desolation forever. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/

## Elam (vv. 34–39)

**v. 34**
- **Cundall (quoted by Guzik):** Elam, more than 200 miles east of Babylonia, is the most distant nation Jeremiah addresses.
- **Thompson (quoted by Guzik):** a broken Babylonian record may describe a clash with Elam in 596/4 BC, which this 597 BC oracle would predate.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Bridgeway:** the oracle showed that Zedekiah's anti-Babylon alliances were wasted effort. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-38.html

**v. 35**
- **Guzik:** the Elamites were famous archers, so their greatest strength becomes their weak point. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/

**vv. 36–37**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** the "four winds" mean Elam will be attacked from every side and scattered everywhere. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-38.htm

**v. 38**
- **Pulpit:** the "throne" means God's tribunal, and Elam loses its native rulers altogether. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-38.htm
- **Ellicott:** the throne is Nebuchadnezzar's, as God's instrument. Shushan, in Elam, later became a royal city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-38.htm
- **Calvin:** God "sets his throne" when he acts as Judge. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-38.html
- **Clarke:** this means either Nebuchadnezzar or Cyrus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-38.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** the oracle never mentions Nebuchadnezzar, and history records no war of his against Elam. Elam stands for the wider pagan world, judged so that it may come to know the true God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/49-38.htm

**v. 39**
- **Clarke:** possibly the spiritual freedom which these people would receive under the Gospel dispensation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-49.html
- **Guzik:** links it to the Elamites present at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-49/
- **Constable (dispensational):** refers it to the end-times future. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-49.html
- **Bridgeway:** Elam became part of Persia, which later conquered Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-38.html
- **Pulpit sermon notes:** the promise is not a literal return of Elam's old glory and must be taken spiritually. https://biblehub.com/sermons/jeremiah/49-38.htm
- **Popular modern use (a BibleHub question page):** points to church growth in Iran today, saying converts routinely report visions of Christ and miraculous healings. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_I_will_set_My_throne_in_Elam.htm

---

## Where the traditions differ

The real disagreement is over how the restoration promises (vv. 2, 6, 39) come true. StudyLight labels the commentators by tradition (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/49-38.html):
- **Clarke** (Arminian, Wesleyan/Methodist) reads v. 39 as gospel freedom.
- **Gill** (Calvinist Baptist) expects a future conversion of the Jews.
- **Calvin** (Reformed) sees fulfilment in Christ's kingdom.
- **Constable** (dispensational) and **Chuck Smith** (Calvary Chapel) look to the end-times future.

A second disagreement concerns Edom's future. Feinberg says no restoration is foretold, while the Pulpit Commentary sees a future for the people in v. 11.

## Not found

I found nothing from Lutheran, Anglican or Pentecostal-denominational sources, nothing from the Catholic or Orthodox sites, nothing from the NET Bible or Bible Odyssey, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
